activities.anchor: that share the wires statistically, instead of reserving a
activities.caption: call the packet count for one file
activities.name: netPacketsEst

config.prompt: A 10 MB file chopped into ~1,460-byte packets — roughly how many packets set off?
config.why: About 7,180 — no circuit to hold idle, so capacity is shared among bursty users; packets may take different routes and arrive out of order, duplicated, or not at all.
config.context: Best-effort inside, guarantees assembled at the edges.

activities.caption: which curve is TCP's congestion behaviour?
activities.name: netSawtoothTrace

config.prompt: Sending rate against round trips for one polite sender — which curve is it?
config.why: Each sender roughly doubles its rate every round trip until packets drop, then cuts back sharply and probes upward — and the shared links divide themselves by feedback, not central control.

activities.anchor: Now the whole trace for one page load
activities.caption: assemble the 200 milliseconds in order
activities.name: netAssemblyOrder

config.prompt: Put the assembly line of one page load in order:
items: DNS — example.com becomes an IP (~20 ms, usually cached)
TCP handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: 'may I?' 'yes,' 'starting' (1 round trip)
TLS handshake — certificate checked, session keys derived (1–2 round trips)
HTTP request/response — GET /, HTML arrives, the browser fires requests for every image, stylesheet and script
config.why: Every click repeats the last three steps — which is why performance work is mostly fewer round trips, smaller payloads and caching.

activities.anchor: layering is both the internet's strength and its attack surface map
activities.caption: file each threat by the floor it hits
activities.name: netLayerSort

config.prompt: File each threat by the floor it hits:

items.label: DNS hijacking — poisoning the name service

config.why: Each threat targets a floor, and defences must be matched to floors.

activities.anchor: since both are sold as speed
activities.caption: true or false — the two performance axes
activities.name: netSpeedJudge

statements.s: Upgrading to a faster connection makes everything feel snappier.
statements.why: Bandwidth and latency are independent — every interactive exchange still pays the same fixed round-trip tax.

statements.s: A 1 GB file over a 100 Mbps link takes about 80 seconds, and no protocol genius changes that.
Light in fibre travels about 200,000 km/s, setting a floor no purchase lifts.
statements.why: Earth's circumference is not negotiable — round-trip time to the far side stays ~150 ms.

statements.s: Bandwidth got cheap while the round trip to the far side of Earth shrank proportionally.
statements.why: Bandwidth grew 1000× in two decades; the round trip never moved — physics, not engineering.

activities.anchor: the zoo shares one addressing trick
activities.caption: pair each port with its tenant
activities.name: netPortMatch

config.prompt: 16-bit numbers multiplex every service over one address — pair each with its tenant:

pairs.right: IMAP — fetching mail to your device

config.why: Email's anatomy shows the layering: SMTP relays between servers, IMAP fetches, MIME carries attachments — protocols composed, not fused.

activities.caption: slide to the floor where TCP lives
activities.name: netStackPlace

config.prompt: The debugging ritual walks the stack from the bottom upward. Slide the marker to the floor where TCP/UDP lives.
config.why: Transport: bytes moved reliably (TCP) or fast and unreliably (UDP) between programs — and 'isolate the failing floor' debugs distributed systems generally.
